title: Scope and surface survey
audience: Trainee or new worker on the pressure cleaning (all heights) track, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Separate low-pressure cleaning from regulated industrial jetting; confirm owner approval, site scope and exclusions.

instruction.heading: Low-pressure cleaning is not regulated jetting
instruction.body: The first decision on any pressure cleaning job is which kind of work it is. Routine exterior cleaning with a domestic or light commercial cleaner is one kind of work. High-pressure water jetting is another, and it carries a different level of risk. WorkSafe Victoria warns that a water jet can pierce skin and inject contaminated material into the body. Its alert sorts equipment by output in bar litres per minute. Class A covers outputs of 800 to 5,600 bar litres per minute, and Class B covers outputs above 5,600, which the alert describes as presenting a higher risk to the operator. The alert points to AS/NZS 4233.1:2013 for the classes, and says Class B operators must be trained and assessed through a registered training organisation. This lesson does not authorise any jetting at that level. The scope agreed with the owner must say which kind of work is being offered, and any request for industrial jetting, hazardous remediation or Class B equipment is outside this course.

instruction.heading: Confirm the owner's approval and the scope
instruction.body: Before a job is accepted, establish what is to be cleaned, why it needs cleaning, and what a successful result looks like. Record the address, the surface materials, the area that can be reached, the nearby drains, the people and vehicles on site, any landscaping that may be damaged, and the owner's restrictions. A pressure cleaner is not the default answer. Some surfaces need a rinse at low pressure, some need manual cleaning, and some need a specialist. Put the scope and the exclusions in writing before the work starts. The price is part of the scope. Western Australian consumer guidance says an accepted quote forms a binding contract, and that extra work needs the customer's approval before it is done. The Northern Territory guidance says a quote can become binding once it forms part of a contract, and that no charge applies for extra work unless it was approved. A change to the scope is therefore a new approval, not a line added at the end of the day.

instruction.heading: Survey the surface before any water is used
instruction.body: Ask the owner about the age of the material, any protective coating, previous leaks, loose pointing, painted sections and past damage. Walk the whole site, not only the area to be cleaned, because runoff, spray and access routes reach beyond it. Look for cracked or loose render, lifting paint, open joints, damaged downpipes and any exposed electrical equipment. Older painted surfaces need a particular check, because paint can contain lead. Photograph each defect with the owner's permission, and mark the excluded zones on a simple site plan. Decide whether the work can be done by the worker, needs a licensed contractor, or needs another specialist, and record that decision before the equipment is unloaded.

instruction.heading: Work at height and the licence position
instruction.body: Work above ground level is a separate question from pressure cleaning. Safe Work Australia defines high risk construction work as construction work with a fall risk of more than 2 metres, and the control order puts a fall prevention device first, then a work positioning system, then a fall arrest system. In New South Wales a safe work method statement is needed where a fall could be more than 2 metres, and a scaffold licence is needed to erect or alter a scaffold where the fall or falling-object risk is more than 4 metres. South Australia moves the high-risk threshold from 3 metres to 2 metres from 1 July 2026. Elevated platforms are a licence question as well. New South Wales: a boom-type elevating work platform needs a WP high risk work licence where the boom length is 11 metres or more (SafeWork NSW, High risk work licences, last modified 15 June 2026 per page metadata). Western Australia: the WP licence covers boom type elevating work platforms with a boom length of 11 metres or more (WorkSafe WA, published 11 August 2026; last updated 13 August 2026). Tasmania: the WP class covers booms of 11 metres or more (WorkSafe Tasmania, Check the classes, last updated 1 December 2023). Northern Territory: the licence class covers boom-type elevating work platforms with a boom length of 11 metres or more (NT WorkSafe bulletin, no date shown). South Australia: no boom-length licence rule is confirmed by an official source; the SafeWork SA high risk work licence page (last updated 10 January 2024) does not name a boom-type elevating work platform class. Queensland: according to the WorkSafe QLD page, search snippet, date not shown, a WP high risk work licence is needed to operate a boom type elevating platform, and elevated work platforms less than 11 metres in length are not included in that definition. Whether a boom-length threshold applies in Victoria is not confirmed by an official source. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start. The national model code measures the boom from the original design, and says that below that length the duty holder still has a duty of care to ensure operators are adequately trained. Scissor lifts do not need the WP licence in Victoria or the Northern Territory.

instruction.heading: Electrical and solar limits
instruction.body: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. In New South Wales, electrical installation work includes repairing and altering an installation. The same page excludes an electrical article that is connected to, and extends beyond, an electrical outlet. Treat every panel and cable as live. Refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

instruction.heading: Stop-work and referral
instruction.body: Stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell the supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain. Stop if wind, rain, ice or fading light changes the conditions, if exposed wiring or water near electrical equipment is seen or suspected, if a person or animal enters the exclusion zone, if the task falls outside your training or the written work order, or if you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or written authorisation the work requires. A stop is not a failure. It is the control working as designed.

procedure: Confirm the type of work requested and whether it is routine low-pressure cleaning, a specialist task or regulated jetting. Stop and refer anything above the scope of this course.
Record the address, the owner's name and the owner's approval of the scope, the price and the exclusions in writing.
Ask the survey questions about material age, coatings, leaks, loose pointing, painted sections and past damage, and record the answers.
Walk the whole site, photograph defects with permission, and mark the excluded zones on a site plan.
Note any work above ground level, any roof or platform access, and any electrical equipment, then decide whether the work needs a licensed contractor or specialist.
Choose the method: low-pressure rinse, manual cleaning, a specialist, or a refusal. Record the reason for the choice.
Put the agreed scope, exclusions and stop-work conditions in writing and obtain the owner's written acceptance before work starts.

workedExamples.situation: A property manager asks for dark staining to be removed from an older painted facade. Open electrical conduits run along the wall, and the manager wants the work started that day. This is an example job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first safe action, and who must be told?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not start. Make the area safe, and tell the supervisor and the property manager that the scope cannot be accepted until the survey is complete. The survey must check the coating condition, because painted surfaces may contain lead, and it must check the open conduits, which are an electrical hazard that a licensed electrician must address. A trial area is needed before any method is chosen. Record why the work was postponed and the conditions needed before it can start.

workedExamples.situation: A customer asks for a tiled roof to be cleaned so it looks new. The roof is steep, and the cleaner would have to climb a ladder to reach it. This is an example job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the roof within the scope you can accept, and what do you say?
workedExamples.reasoning: Not as a routine pressure clean. Roof access is work above ground level, and it needs the authorisation and any licence the state requires. Exclude the roof from the scope, offer the ground-level work that is in scope, and refer the roof to a specialist with the appropriate authority. Record the exclusion and the customer's written acceptance.

workedExamples.situation: A customer wants a driveway cleaned as well as the house, after the house scope was agreed in writing. The extra area is not in the quote. This is an example job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What must you do before cleaning the driveway?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop, record the request, and ask for the customer's approval of the extra work and its price before doing it. Extra work that was not in the accepted quote needs approval first. If the customer declines, the driveway stays out of scope and the decision is recorded.

equipmentAndPpe: Site survey form or digital record, with the scope, exclusions and owner approval
Site plan or sketch for marking excluded zones and access routes
Camera or phone for defect photographs, used only with the owner's permission
Measuring tape for recording areas and distances to drains and boundaries
Closed footwear with good grip and high-visibility clothing for any site walk
Eye protection for anyone near cleaning activity during the survey

commonErrors.error: Accepting a job before the scope, the exclusions and the owner's approval are in writing.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the scope and exclusions, and obtain written acceptance before work begins.

commonErrors.error: Treating pressure as the default method for every surface.
commonErrors.prevention: Choose the method after the survey, and record why a method was chosen or rejected.

commonErrors.error: Surveying only the area to be cleaned.
commonErrors.prevention: Walk the whole site, including drains, access routes and any electrical equipment.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a licence or authority covers the work because the cleaner is confident.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and authorisation position for the state before any work above ground level.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Working above ground level: the fall threshold, control order and licence positions are set out in the instruction above. Check the position for the state and the employer's written authorisation before any work above ground level. This lesson does not grant that authority.

Boom-type elevating work platforms, state by state: New South Wales, where the WP licence applies at a boom length of 11 metres or more (SafeWork NSW, last modified 15 June 2026 per page metadata); Western Australia, where the WP licence covers a boom length of 11 metres or more (WorkSafe WA, last updated 13 August 2026); Tasmania, where the WP class covers booms of 11 metres or more (WorkSafe Tasmania, last updated 1 December 2023); the Northern Territory, where the licence class covers a boom length of 11 metres or more (NT WorkSafe bulletin, no date shown); South Australia, where no boom-length licence rule is confirmed by an official source; and Queensland, where the WorkSafe QLD page, search snippet, date not shown, says that elevated work platforms less than 11 metres in length are not included in the boom-type definition. The national model code uses the same length. Whether a boom-length threshold applies in Victoria is not confirmed by an official source. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start.
Electrical work: this lesson does not permit work on solar or electrical installations.
Completing this lesson is not a licence, a certificate or an authority for regulated work.

qualityStandard: The scope, the reason for cleaning and the success measure are confirmed with the owner in writing before acceptance.
The address, surface materials, accessible area, drains, people, vehicles, landscaping and owner restrictions are recorded.
Excluded zones are marked on a site plan, and the need for a licensed contractor or specialist is decided and recorded.
Defects are photographed only with the owner's permission, and extra work is approved before it is done.
documentationEvidence: Signed or written scope record with owner approval, price basis and exclusions
Survey record with the material, coating, leak and damage answers, and the defect photographs taken with permission
Site plan with excluded zones, access routes and drains marked
Method decision record with the reason for the choice, and any referral
summary: Separate routine low-pressure cleaning from regulated jetting, and say which kind of work is offered.
Confirm the owner's approval, the scope, the exclusions and the price in writing before work starts.
Survey the whole site, mark the excluded zones, and refer work above ground level, electrical work or specialist surfaces.
This lesson alone does not authorise regulated jetting, hazardous remediation, electrical work or work at height.

knowledgeChecks.question: What must be confirmed before accepting the scope of a pressure cleaning job?
options: The owner's approval, surface materials, exclusions, and whether a licensed contractor or specialist is needed
That a pressure cleaner is the default tool for every surface, so the owner's approval can wait until the work is under way
That the customer has paid the full price before the site is walked and the scope is written down
That the work can start at height if the cleaner feels confident and has the right ladder on site

knowledgeChecks.question: The customer has accepted a quote, and asks for an extra section that is not in it. What is correct?
options: Clean the extra section and bill for it later, since the customer will agree
Ask for the customer's approval of the extra work and its price before doing it
Add the section and charge the difference only if the customer complains
Treat the accepted quote as non-binding so the price can change as the job goes

knowledgeChecks.question: During the site walk, an older painted surface and an open electrical conduit are found next to the work area. What comes first?
options: Start cleaning the area away from the conduit, since the conduit is not in the spray path of the jet today
Stop, keep people clear, record the findings, and tell the supervisor and owner before any work near the conduit
Cover the conduit with tape and continue the cleaning as planned for the day, since the tape will protect the wires
Test the paint with a high-pressure jet to see how it reacts before any other work is planned at the site
